Section. Introduction. Tableaux are certain (downward-branching) trees of signed formulas, that is, pairs consisting of a truth value sign ( true sign or false sign ) and a sentence Displayed expression. true A or false A. End displayed expression. A tableau begins with a number of assumptions. Each further signed formula is generated by applying one of the inference rules. Some inference rules add one or more signed formulas to a tip of the tree; others add two new tips, resulting in two branches. Rules result in signed formulas where the formula is less complex than that of the signed formula to which it was applied. When a branch contains both true formula A and false formula A , we say the branch is closed. If every branch in a tableau is closed, the entire tableau is closed. A closed tableau constitutes a derivation that shows that the set of signed formulas which were used to begin the tableau are unsatisfiable. listen_text: Section. Simple Tableaux for Sfive. Sfive is sound and complete with respect to the class of universal models, that is, models where every world is accessible from every world. In universal models the accessibility relation doesn't matter: “there is a world world w where formula A is true at world w in model M ” is true if and only if there is such a world w that's accessible from world u . So in Sfive, we can define models as simply a set of worlds and a valuation V . This suggests that we should be able to simplify the tableau rules as well. In the general case, we take as prefixes sequences of positive integers, so that we can keep track of which such prefixes name worlds which are accessible from others: prefix sigma dot n names a world accessible from prefix sigma . But in Sfive any world is accessible from any world, so there is no need to so keep track. Instead, we can use positive integers as prefixes. To show that the method of tableaux is complete, we have to show that whenever there is no closed tableau to show Gamma derives formula A , then Gamma does not semantically entail formula A , that is, there is a countermodel. But “there is no closed tableau” means that every way we could try to construct one has to fail to close. The trick is to see that if every such way fails to close, then a specific, systematic and exhaustive way also fails to close. And this systematic and exhaustive way would close if a closed tableau exists. The single tableau will contain, among its open branches, all the information required to define a countermodel. The countermodel given by an open branch in this tableau will contain the all the prefixes used on that branch as the worlds, and a propositional variable p is true at prefix sigma if and only if true p at prefix sigma occurs on the branch. The proof of the completeness theorem doesn't just show that if formula A is semantically valid then formula A is derivable , it also gives us a method for constructing countermodels to formula A if the source expression A, without a formula marker, is not semantically valid . In the case of logic K , this method constitutes a decision procedure. For suppose formula A is not semantically valid . Then the proof of the proposition that every finite Gamma has a complete tableau gives a method for constructing a complete tableau. The method in fact always terminates. The propositional rules for logic K only add prefixed formulas of lower complexity, that is, each propositional rule need only be applied once on a branch for any signed formula with sign S formula A at prefix sigma . New prefixes are only generated by the false necessity rule and true possibility rules, and also only have to be applied once (and produce a single new prefix). true necessity rule and false possibility rule have to be applied potentially multiple times, but only once per prefix, and only finitely many new prefixes are generated. So the construction either results in a closed branch or a complete branch after finitely many stages. Source anomaly note. Source caveat.
